prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms held at a magic wavelength give frequency standards of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks (B049) to Katori and Ye. I came to this ballot from outside the field of precision metrology, and what persuades me is the physics at the level of detail I care about. The magic-wavelength condition cancels the lattice light shift on the clock transition, which leaves many atoms Doppler- and recoil-free. That is a new regime, not the same regime as the comb or the single ion. The numbers have been reproduced: uncertainties near 1e-18 at several laboratories, cross-continental comparisons that agree, and density and blackbody shifts that are understood quantitatively. The discussion also answers my own round-1 worry. Six of eight members now carry B049, and the support comes from members with different tastes, so it does not rest on one subfield's enthusiasm. The remaining objections concern attribution and prize history, not the experimental result. I would write the citation around the concept and its realization, and I would say so explicitly in the public text, so that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is addressed directly and the prize is not read as a general award for precision timekeeping or for either laureate's career.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is still the question the chair raised: is this a discovery, or an instrument with a very good number? Lindroth, Danielsson and Kroll all note that no surprising new phenomenon has appeared in the data, and the scientific harvest (geodesy at scale, constants tests, dark-matter limits, a redefined second) is partly prospective. I accept that. My answer is that the Nobel record contains instrument-enabled discoveries where the enabling idea itself opened new physics, and the many-atom magic-wavelength interrogation with controlled many-body shifts qualifies, but a colleague who weights measured departures from known physics heavily can reasonably disagree. The credit is also not airtight: Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat and Ludlow made real contributions and Ye's role is partly performance leadership. Olsson's question whether Katori alone would stand is fair. I would not accept Katori alone, because the result that convinced the community was the 1e-18 systematics and the many-body control, and these are Ye's. Finally, I do not accept a weaker second part to fill space, and I prefer one part over two.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the prize would stand on Katori alone, given that Katori holds the original proposal and first realization while Ye took the platform to record accuracy, and she wants the citation to credit the clock work and not a general career.
responses.response: I agree with the last point and have written my citation that way. On the first, I would keep both names. The magic-wavelength proposal is the idea, but the community accepted it as a clock only after the systematics were pushed to the 1e-18 level and the density-dependent shifts, which could have undermined the scheme, were shown to be controllable. That control is the physical content that makes the lattice clock a result in a new regime and not a proposal. So the concept and its first realization belong to Katori, and the demonstration that the concept actually works at the frontier belongs to Ye. If the committee judged Ye's part purely as execution, I would find the question harder, but I do not see it that way.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B049 at the centre and adds B047 (Halzen alone, IceCube) as a second part, while saying the second part is droppable and the fallback is B049 alone or B049 with B024.
responses.response: I respect that you named the weakness of your own second part, and I agree with your fallback. IceCube is a real new window, but I cannot defend a one-person credit for a collaboration of hundreds from the supplied material, and nobody else has argued that it can. I am not in a position to judge the astrophysics, so I defer to you and Danielsson on whether the source identifications are mature. For credit alone I would keep the prize as a single part. A second part should be added only if a defensible one-to-three-person attribution is shown, and nobody has shown it. My preferred configuration therefore does not include a second part.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that theta-13 is a clue from nature that nobody could have deduced and that it opened leptonic CP violation, and he rates B024 as the thinnest in breadth of support while worrying about the overlap with the 2015 prize.
responses.response: Your framing of B024 as a measurement of something nature surprised us with is the strongest version of the discovery-versus-instrument argument against my own choice, and I take it seriously. I defer on the particle physics. My concern is the same one you raise: the 2015 prize is close, and three spokesperson names have to stand for Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz, with the accelerator appearance results outside. I keep B024 out of my alternatives for that reason, not because of its quality, and I would support discussing it if B049 fails on the 2005 and 2012 overlap.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B048 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a mature and independently confirmed discovery, and did not make B038 an alternative because of the one-year gap since the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize.
responses.response: I accept your reasoning on B038, and on the 2025 cycle you have more direct knowledge than I do. I have therefore removed B038 from my alternatives and will not argue for it. On B048, I cannot verify HgTe edge-conductance reproduction outside the Molenkamp group, as you say, but the Z2 classification and its experimental test seem to me to be a clean theory-plus-experiment story. I have put it in my alternatives in place of B038. My remaining worry is the one you list, that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are left out, and that the citation must be compound.

responses.point: Kroll answered that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes concerns framing and not eligibility, and that the prior prizes cover the comb and single-ion control but not the neutral-atom many-particle lattice clock.
responses.response: Thank you; I agree with that distinction and I have used it in my citation. I would add that your remark about my own reservation was fair: I applied a stricter overlap test to the lattice clock than to circuit QED, and the 2025 circuits prize is the closer overlap. That is one of the reasons I now rank B049 above B038 and recuse from B038.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a discovery-class advance (a new regime with controlled many-body systematics) and not an instrument performance record; no measured departure from known physics has yet appeared.
Whether Ye's contribution is weighted as concept-level (many-body control and the 1e-18 demonstration) or as execution, which determines whether the credit is Katori and Ye or Katori alone.

Whether other contributors (Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat, Ludlow) can be omitted without distorting the credit, and whether the citation wording makes the boundary with the 2005 and 2012 prizes clear enough.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second matters for timing; I do not treat it as a precondition.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work at Chalmers MC2 in superconducting circuits, so I recuse myself from any discussion and vote on B038 (circuit QED), which I opened with, and I flag that B044 (trapped-ion quantum computing) is adjacent to my programme. I have no tie to Katori or Ye or to the lattice-clock community apparent from my profile. Mehlig and Olsson are Chalmers colleagues, with no specific collaboration. I have taken B038 out of my alternatives and list B044 only as a fallback.
